periods.activity_title: Into the Toy Shop — Read-Aloud and First Look

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.49): name toys in the shop; identify the train the boy requested.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story aloud from the opening market scene through the toy kitten spotting the two window-shopping girls (Textbook pp.44–48), pausing at the pictures to name toys visible. Students follow along with fingers on the page.

Teacher continues the read-aloud through the story's end (pp.48–49), giving distinct voices to the toy kitten, the talking doll, the toy elephant, the toy aeroplane, and the toy phone. Students listen and watch for which toy each customer chooses.

Let us think — A: students answer the two questions orally in turn — listing all toys stocked in the shop and naming the Vande Bharat toy train the little boy asked for. Teacher confirms answers by pointing to relevant passages in the text (p.49).
Quick whole-class recall: teacher holds up the book and points to each toy in the story; students call out its name aloud, building a running mental inventory of the shop.

periods.teacher_notes: The story gives voice to toys' feelings — draw students' attention to words like 'eagerly', 'sigh', and 'hopes' as the read-aloud proceeds so they begin to notice that the narrator is inside the toys' minds. Students may initially list only two or three toys; prompt them by asking about wooden toys, soft toys, board games, and specific named toys such as Snakes and Ladders, the dancing dolls, and the spinning top.
materials: Blackboard or chart with the word 'Vande Bharat' written clearly

periods.activity_title: Toy Feelings and 'My Top' — Listen, Speak, Repeat

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.49): paired talk on toy feelings and the Jaadui Pitara.
Let us listen — A (p.51): listen and repeat the poem 'My Top' with the teacher.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the story's emotional thread — the toy elephant hoping to be chosen, the toys sighing when customers walk past — to prime students to think about their own feelings around toys.

Let us think — B, Question 1: students turn to a partner and talk about how they feel when someone buys or gives a toy to them. Two or three pairs share with the class; teacher gathers a short board list of feeling words (happy, excited, surprised, loved).

Let us think — B, Question 2: whole-class brief discussion on the 'Jaadui Pitara' — who has seen it, what it contains, how it connects to the idea of toys as learning tools. Teacher accepts all responses warmly.
Teacher reads the poem 'My Top' aloud at normal pace (p.51), holding up the textbook. Students listen with eyes on the page, noticing the colour words and the movement described.

Listening and repeating: teacher recites 'My Top' line by line three to four times; students repeat each line in chorus, then the full poem together. Teacher invites individual students to recite the final two lines alone, building confidence with repetition.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem 'My Top' uses simple rhyme and repetition — 'round and round' appears twice and the child 'jumps around' to mirror the top — so students can join in quickly. For the paired talk on toy feelings, encourage students to use complete sentences rather than single words; model one example yourself ('I feel very happy when someone gives me a toy because it means they care about me.').
materials: Blackboard with feeling words written during discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.50): add a describing word from the help box to each naming word.
Let us learn — B (p.50): write the plural by adding 's' to five naming words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'happy boy', 'pretty doll', 'blue frock', 'red cap' on the board, drawing these directly from the story. Students identify which word in each pair tells us more about the naming word; teacher introduces the term 'describing word' in context.

Let us learn — A: teacher writes the five naming words (food, kurta, water, paper, tree) on the board and reads the help box aloud. Students choose a describing word for each and write it in their notebooks; two or three students share answers while the class judges whether the choice makes sense in a real sentence.

Teacher connects to the story: 'toy → toys', 'boy → boys'. Students say both forms aloud together, then teacher introduces the rule that we add 's' for more than one thing and writes the word 'plural' on the board.

Let us learn — B: students write the plural of cat, cup, doll, shop, and train in their notebooks by adding 's'. Teacher circulates; a student volunteer writes each answer on the board, and the class reads the plural word aloud in unison to confirm.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often attach any describing word without checking meaning; anchor each answer back to a real sentence ('Can you have cold water? Yes! Can you have cold paper? What do you think?'). The story's own language — 'a red cap', 'a talking doll', 'a wooden toy' — gives you ready-made examples of describing words in action that students will recognise from the read-aloud.

periods.activity_title: Plurals with '-es' and Colour Words in the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — C (p.51): write the plural by adding 'es' to five naming words.
Let us listen — B (p.52): circle the colour words from 'My Top' in the given list.

time_bands.activity: Quick warm-up: teacher calls out singular nouns from the previous plural work (toys, boys, dolls) and students say the singular. Then teacher writes 'box → boxes' on the board and asks why we cannot just add 's'. Students offer ideas; teacher guides them to hear the extra syllable and introduces the '-es' rule.

Let us learn — C: students write the plurals of class, bus, pouch, brush, and mango in their notebooks using '-es'. Teacher writes each answer on the board as students volunteer; the class reads each plural word aloud, clapping the syllables to hear why '-es' is needed.
Teacher re-reads the poem 'My Top' aloud once while students follow (p.51–52). Students listen specifically for colour words; teacher then asks: 'Which colours did you hear? Keep them in your head.'

Let us listen — B: students open to p.52, read the eight colour words in the box, and circle only those that appear in the poem 'My Top'. Students compare with a partner; teacher reveals the answer (red, green, yellow, brown) by asking volunteers to read out the poem line by line.

periods.teacher_notes: The '-es' rule applies to words ending in s, x, ch, sh, and some words ending in o — students at this stage need to hear and feel the reason rather than memorise a list of endings, so the syllable-clapping activity is important. The colour-word task ties word work back to the poem students have already heard and repeated, giving the vocabulary a familiar anchor.

periods.activity_title: Making a Kite — Sentence Completion from Pictures

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.53): complete the four kite-making sentences using picture clues.

time_bands.activity: Teacher conducts a picture walk through the six illustrations on p.52–53 — baby bird in the nest, mother flying to collect materials, collecting spider-web thread, gathering tree gum, getting a palm-leaf blade, and the baby bird flying the kite. Students describe what they see in each picture using single words or short phrases.

Teacher reads the clue box aloud (little chick, kite, onion peel, thread from spider web, gum from a tree, leaf blade from the palm tree) and models completing the first sentence on the board: 'The mother bird brought onion peel from onions.' Students copy the modelled sentence and discuss what comes next.

Students complete the remaining three sentences — 'Then, she ___', 'Next, the mother bird ___', 'Finally, ___' — independently in their notebooks, using the picture clues and the help words. Teacher circulates and supports students who need help connecting a picture to a clue word.

Three to four volunteers read their completed sentences aloud; the class follows along on p.53 to check the sequence. Teacher affirms correct answers and gently corrects any clue-word mismatches, then students copy any corrections neatly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may want to write full invented sentences rather than use the given clue words; redirect them gently by pointing to the clue box and asking 'Can you find a word in the box that matches this picture?' The sequence of the pictures drives the sequence of the sentences, so encourage students to number the pictures 1–6 before writing.

periods.activity_title: Letter into Bird — Step-by-Step Drawing and Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — B (p.54): follow seven steps to draw a bird from the letter 'B' and colour it.
Let us write — C (p.54–55): draw a picture using any other letter and label it.

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the completed bird drawing from the textbook (p.54) and asks students what letter they can see hidden in the bird's body. Students identify the capital letter 'B' and examine how the two loops became the body.

Let us write — B: teacher demonstrates each of the seven steps on the board one at a time, pausing after each for students to complete that step in their notebooks. Steps proceed from writing the capital 'B', adding the beak and eye, drawing the wing, adding the tail, and finishing with feet and a branch. Students colour the bird when all seven steps are complete.

Let us write — C: students choose any other letter of the alphabet and attempt to turn it into a picture, drawing and colouring freely. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to think about what shape the letter reminds them of — a 'C' could be a crescent moon, an 'S' could be a snake.

Quick share: three or four students hold up their letter-pictures and the class guesses which letter was used. Teacher celebrates all attempts and notes the creativity of the connection between letter shape and picture.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who rush ahead of the modelled steps often end up with a confused outline; keep each step brief and wait for the class before moving to the next. The letter-to-picture task is open-ended by design — accept any letter and any picture provided the connection to the letter shape is visible, even loosely.

periods.activity_title: Making a Jute or Cardboard Puppet

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — Jute/Cardboard Puppets (p.55): make a face puppet following the eight-step guide.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the puppet-making to the story: the toys in the shop all have faces and feelings — today students will make a toy face of their own. Teacher shows the completed puppet image on p.55 and reads the materials list aloud so students know what they are working with.

Teacher distributes jute sheets or cardboard sheets and other materials. Students write their name on the back of their sheet so pieces are not confused. Teacher reads Steps 1–3 aloud (take the sheet, draw a human face outline, cut it out) and demonstrates on a spare piece of cardboard.

Students work through Steps 4–7 at their own pace: drawing features, colouring, adding woollen thread for hair, and attaching a cardboard handle at the back. Teacher circulates, helping with cutting and gluing and prompting students to decide what expression — happy, surprised, thoughtful — their puppet will have.

Puppet share: students hold up their finished puppets and give them a voice — each student says one sentence as their puppet ('Hello! I am Mia and I love spinning tops!'). Classmates listen and respond with a thumbs-up for puppets that remind them of characters from the story.

Brief reflection: teacher asks two or three students which toy from the story their puppet most resembles and why. Students make the connection between handmade craft and the traditional Indian toys — Chennapatna, Kondapalli — mentioned in the story, closing the chapter's imaginative loop.

periods.teacher_notes: Cutting cardboard can be slow at Grade III; pre-cut outlines or lightly scored lines on cardboard sheets will help students focus on the creative steps rather than struggling with scissors. If jute sheets are unavailable, thick paper or old cereal-box cardboard works equally well — the craft outcome matters more than the specific material.
materials: Jute sheets or cardboard sheets (one per student)
A spare cardboard piece for teacher demonstration

items.source_lo: Student retrieves explicit information and identifies characters and events using a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Toy shop story; named toys; Vande Bharat train; customers making choices.
items.item_stem:
Read the sentences below. Write T if the sentence is true and F if it is false.
1. The toy shop in the story opens at 9 a.m.
2. The first two girls who come to the shop buy the toy aeroplane.
3. A little boy asks his mother for the Vande Bharat toy train.
4. The spinning top is chosen by a girl in a red cap.

options.text: The toy shop in the story opens at 9 a.m.
The first two girls who come to the shop buy the toy aeroplane.
A little boy asks his mother for the Vande Bharat toy train.
The spinning top is chosen by a girl in a red cap.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 – T (the shop opens at 9 a.m.); 2 – F (the first two girls only window-shop and walk away; the toy aeroplane is bought by one of a later pair of girls); 3 – T (the little boy asks his mother for the Vande Bharat toy train); 4 – F (it is a boy wearing a red cap who takes the spinning top, not a girl).

items.source_lo: Student retrieves explicit information and identifies characters and events using a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Toy shop story; named toys; Vande Bharat train; customers making choices.
items.item_stem: In the story, many customers visit the toy shop and each person chooses something different. Think about the last group of children who enter the shop. Who picks the toy elephant? What does the boy in the red cap choose? Write your answer in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: A girl from the last group of children picks the toy elephant. The boy in the red cap chooses a spinning top.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively, repeats a short rhyme, and expresses personal responses using spoken language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Poem 'My Top'; toy feelings paired talk; Jaadui Pitara discussion.
items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the poem 'My Top' aloud once. Listen carefully. Then choose the correct answer.
Which movement does the child make while watching the top spin?

options.label: A
options.text: The child sits very still and watches.

options.label: D
options.text: The child lies down on the floor.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student heard the stillness of watching but missed the action word 'jump around'.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student may have guessed a lively action without attending to the poem's exact word.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student did not connect the top's spinning motion to the child's described response.

items.item_stem:
Look at Textbook page 53. The pictures show a mother bird making a kite for her baby bird. Use the words in the box to fill in the blanks and complete the sentences.

Word box: spider web, gum, palm leaf blade, peel
items.visual_stimulus:
| Blank | Complete the sentence |
|---|---|
| 1 | The mother bird brought ___ from onions. |
| 2 | Then, she found thread from a ___. |
| 3 | Next, she collected ___ from a tree. |
| 4 | Finally, she used a ___ to make the kite frame. |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 – peel; 2 – spider web; 3 – gum; 4 – palm leaf blade.

expected_elements: Writes from the baby bird's point of view.
Includes at least one feeling word.
Describes something seen or experienced while flying.
